sound: Start with an open a and glide toward i within one syllable. There is no consonant initial, and the tone mark belongs on a, not i.
contrast: 爱 and 矮 differ in tone, not in the written letters ai. 挨 has an additional ái reading in words about enduring; āi here is the close-to sense.
practice: Contrast 爱 (love) with 矮 (short). Copy both, then cover the pinyin and recall which one has the falling fourth tone.

sound: Close the lips and release b without the strong puff used for p. Pinyin b is not the same voiced sound as English b in every context; keep the final a open.
contrast: 八, 拔, and 爸 give first-, second-, and fourth-tone examples. Sentence-final 吧 is usually neutral ba and is not the same word as 爸.
practice: Write 八 and 爸 in alternating rows, then add 拔. Say the tone before tracing rather than attaching the same pitch to every ba.

sound: Release the lips for b, then finish en with the tongue touching behind the upper teeth for n. Do not add a g-like ending.
contrast: 本 and 笨 contrast third and fourth tone. 奔 is bēn for running, but bèn occurs for heading toward a destination; learn the whole word.
practice: Practise 一本书 and the character 本 first. Compare its sound with 笨, noticing that a matching base spelling does not make the meanings similar.

sound: Keep the lips rounded for u after the short unaspirated b release. This u is different from the front rounded ü in 女 nǚ.
contrast: These examples all have lexical fourth tone. 不 changes to bú before another fourth-tone syllable, as in 不是 bú shì; the character's dictionary reading remains bù.
practice: Make three rows for 不, 布, and 步. Read 不好 and 不是 aloud before writing to separate the dictionary tone from the phrase-level change.

sound: The ch initial is retroflex and aspirated. The written i after ch is not the ee-like vowel of ji; keep the tongue in the retroflex position.
contrast: 吃, 迟, and 尺 provide three different tones. 尺 here names a ruler or length unit and is chǐ; special musical uses can have another reading.
practice: Practise 吃 and 迟 as a listening contrast, then copy 尺. Keep the same consonant and change pitch, rather than changing chi into qi.

sound: Start d with the tongue near the upper teeth and little released air. It contrasts with aspirated t; a stays open and carries the tone mark.
contrast: 大, 打, and 答 contrast fourth, third, and second tone. 答 is dá in 回答, but dā appears in some other words such as 答应.
practice: Read 大 and 打 as a pair, then practise 回答. Use the worksheet to connect each tone to a different character instead of one generic da symbol.

sound: The final e is a back unrounded vowel, not English dee. Neutral de is short and light; it does not need a written tone mark.
contrast: 的 is neutral in ordinary possessive phrases. 得 is dé for obtaining but de in some complements and děi for must; that last reading belongs to dei, a different syllable.
practice: Write 我的 and 得到 as separate examples. Keep de and dé distinct and do not assume every character written 得 has the same pronunciation.

sound: Use the unaspirated d initial followed by an ee-like i. The fourth-tone mark replaces the dot above i in dì.
contrast: 地 is dì for ground or place, but de as an adverbial particle. 第 and 弟 are also dì, showing that one syllable and tone can match several characters.
practice: Practise 地, 第, and 弟 together. Say a word such as 地图, 第一, or 弟弟 so the context tells you which homophone to write.

sound: Start with d and keep u rounded through the syllable. A rising tone makes dú; a falling tone makes dù without changing the vowel.
contrast: 读 is dú for reading. 都 is dū for a capital city, but dōu for all; do not use the dū example to pronounce 都 in 我们都去.
practice: Read 读书 and 首都 before writing 读 and 都. Add 度 as a fourth-tone contrast and keep the two readings of 都 tied to their words.

sound: The g initial is unaspirated and made at the back of the mouth. The final e is not English gee and should not acquire a final y sound. Keep the g distinct from aspirated k, then contrast first-tone gē with fourth-tone gè.
contrast: 哥 and 歌 share gē but differ in meaning and shape. 个 is usually gè in careful counting, can be unstressed in phrases, and has a special gě reading in 自个儿.
practice: Practise 一个 and 哥哥, then write 歌. Use the examples to distinguish tone changes from separate characters with the same first-tone syllable.

sound: After g, glide through a rounded u into o without making two syllables. The tone mark is placed on o in guó, guǒ, and guò.
contrast: 国, 果, and 过 form a useful second-, third-, and fourth-tone set. Aspect-marker 过 is often unstressed guo in speech, unlike the full verb guò.
practice: Make a three-row worksheet for 国, 果, and 过. Recall country, fruit, and pass while reading the different tone marks.

sound: Begin with h and glide from a toward o within one syllable. The tone mark goes on a, the main vowel of ao.
contrast: 好 is hǎo for good and hào for liking something in words such as 爱好. 号 is hào for a number, while háo can occur for shouting.
practice: Compare 你好 with 爱好 before copying 好. Add 号 and 毫 to show why the full word matters even when the base spelling is hao.

sound: Use a gentle h sound followed by the back unrounded vowel e. Do not turn he into the English word he with an ee vowel.
contrast: 喝 is hē for drinking, with other readings in special words. 和 is hé for and or harmony but has several contextual readings; 河 is the river homophone.
practice: Practise 喝水, 我和你, and 河. Sort the examples into hē and hé before printing, then check the left radical of each character.

sound: Round the lips briefly for u, then open into a after h. The glide stays inside one syllable and the tone mark belongs on a.
contrast: 花 contrasts in tone with 话 and 画. The latter two share huà, so pronunciation alone cannot decide whether you mean speech or drawing.
practice: Print 花, 话, and 画. Say 花草, 说话, and 画画 to give each written form enough word context.

sound: The spelling ui abbreviates the final uei after an initial. In huì, the tone mark is on i even though the fuller sound sequence includes e.
contrast: 会, 回, and 灰 contrast fourth, second, and first tone. 会 also has the kuài reading in 会计; that is a separate syllable rather than another hui tone.
practice: Read 会写, 回家, and 灰色 before copying the characters. Keep hui distinct from huai, which has a different vowel sequence.

sound: The j initial is made toward the front of the tongue and is unaspirated. Follow it with an ee-like i; do not substitute English j or retroflex zh.
contrast: 几 is jǐ for how many, but jī for a small table and in certain other words. 鸡 is first tone and 记 is fourth tone; use context to pick the character.
practice: Practise 几个, 鸡, and 记住. Keep jǐ as the question reading and do not transfer a radical's small-table reading into a counting question.

sound: Move from j through a short i glide into a. The syllable has one beat, and the tone mark is written on a rather than i.
contrast: 家 and 加 are homophones in first tone. 假 is jiǎ for false, but jià in holiday or leave words such as 放假.
practice: Write 家 and 加 together, then contrast 假 with the word 放假. The worksheet should help recall both character choice and contextual tone.

sound: Begin with j and end with a clear n closure. Do not turn jin into jing by adding a back-of-mouth nasal ending.
contrast: 今 and 金 share first-tone jīn, while 进 is fourth-tone jìn. Their different shapes and meanings show why pinyin is a reading aid rather than a unique character identifier.
practice: Practise 今天, 金, and 进来. Cover the character column and reconstruct the correct form from each word, not from jin alone.

sound: The k initial is aspirated, with a noticeable puff of air. Finish an with n at the front of the mouth rather than the ng ending of kang.
contrast: 看 is kàn for looking or reading and kān for guarding or looking after. 刊 and 砍 add first- and third-tone examples with different written forms.
practice: Read 看书 and 看门 before writing 看. Add 刊 and 砍, and practise the final n without changing the syllable to kang.

sound: Start with the tongue touching near the upper teeth for l, then glide from a toward i. The tone mark belongs on a.
contrast: 来 and 莱 share lái, while 赖 has a falling fourth tone. 莱 is a plant character often seen in names; it is included as a sound example, not a beginner frequency claim.
practice: Practise 来 first in 来学校, then compare 赖. Use 莱 to notice that different written forms can share exactly the same syllable and tone.

sound: Close the lips for m and open directly into a. Keep the initial and vowel constant while changing pitch or making the syllable neutral.
contrast: 妈, 麻, 马, 骂, and 吗 illustrate first, second, third, fourth, and neutral tone. 麻 is má in 麻木 (numb); the ordinary yes-no question particle 吗 is neutral ma, not má.
practice: Print the five characters. Read 妈妈, 麻木, 马, 骂人, and 好吗, then sort them by their first syllable tone. Keep the question-ending ma light instead of giving it the rising tone of 麻.

sound: Begin with m and glide from a to i. Put the tone mark on a; mai is one syllable, not separate ma and yi.
contrast: 买 and 卖 contrast third and fourth tone and have opposite transaction meanings. 埋 is mái for burying, but mán in 埋怨.
practice: Practise 买书 and 卖书 in alternating rows, then add 埋. Check the extra 十 in 卖 as well as its falling tone.

sound: Start with m and finish ing with a back nasal ng. Keep it distinct from min, whose final n closes near the front of the mouth.
contrast: 明 and 名 are second-tone homophones, while 命 is fourth tone. 明天 and 名字 supply useful contexts for choosing the correct written form.
practice: Print 明, 名, and 命. Read 明天 and 名字 aloud and identify the shared míng without treating the characters as interchangeable.

sound: Use an n initial with the tongue near the upper teeth, followed by an ee-like i. The third-tone mark replaces the dot in nǐ.
contrast: 你, 尼, and 逆 provide third-, second-, and fourth-tone examples. In 你好, the first third tone normally rises before the following third tone, though the written pinyin stays nǐ hǎo.
practice: Start with 你 and 你好, then compare 尼 and 逆. Practise saying the greeting naturally without rewriting its dictionary tone marks.

sound: The Mandarin r initial is not an English r imitation; hold the tongue farther back and finish en with a front n closure.
contrast: 人, 认, and 忍 contrast second, fourth, and third tone. 认识 often has a light second syllable, but the rèn reading of 认 remains identifiable.
practice: Practise 人 and 认识 before copying 认. Add 忍 and focus on changing pitch while preserving the same ren syllable.

sound: The sh initial is retroflex. Its following written i is not the ee-like vowel in xi; keep the tongue back rather than turning shi into shee.
contrast: 师, 时, and 是 form a first-, second-, and fourth-tone set. 十 is another shí character, so tone alone does not uniquely choose between time and ten.
practice: Read 老师, 时间, and 是 before tracing. Add 十 from its guide if you want a same-tone character-choice exercise.

sound: Use retroflex sh followed by the contracted ui final. The tone mark falls on i, as in shuǐ, rather than on u.
contrast: 水 and 睡 contrast third and fourth tone. 谁 can be shuí or shéi; the shéi pronunciation belongs to a different base spelling and is common in speech.
practice: Practise 水 and 睡觉 first, then read 谁 with both accepted pronunciations. Do not invent a first-tone example simply to fill a four-tone chart.

sound: The spelling w introduces a u-like glide into o; it is not treated as one of the 21 consonant initials here. Keep wo in one syllable.
contrast: 我, 窝, and 握 give third-, first-, and fourth-tone examples. An empty second-tone example slot is not permission to invent a word.
practice: Print 我, 窝, and 握. Use 我 as the familiar anchor, then change pitch while keeping the rounded opening glide.

sound: Begin with the front-tongue x sound, then glide through i into e. Mark the tone on e, not on i, in xiè and xiě.
contrast: 谢, 写, and 鞋 contrast fourth, third, and second tone. 谢谢 commonly has a neutral second syllable, xièxie, even though isolated 谢 is xiè.
practice: Practise 谢谢 and 写字 before copying 谢 and 写. Add 鞋 as a second-tone contrast and keep the x sound separate from retroflex sh.

sound: Use the unaspirated retroflex zh initial and finish ong with a back nasal ng. It differs from zong at the beginning and zhong does not end in n.
contrast: 中 is zhōng for middle but zhòng for hitting a target. 种 is zhǒng for kind or seed and zhòng for planting; 重 can also be chóng for again.
practice: Print 中, 钟, 种, and 重. Read 中国, 时钟, 一种, and 很重 so every tone choice has a meaningful word context.
